1. Market Overview & Long-Term Price Trend

Gold rose from ~$274 in August 2000 to ~$5,377 by March 2026 — a cumulative gain of 1,863% (12.4% CAGR). The trajectory encompasses multiple macro regimes: a secular bull market driven by dollar weakness and inflation fears (2001–2011), a deep correction during the strong-dollar/disinflation era (2011–2015), and an explosive rally from pandemic-era stimulus through 2026.

Annual Returns

Gold delivered positive annual returns in 21 of 27 years. The largest annual gain was 62.7% (2025), while the worst year returned -28.8% (2013).

Drawdown Profile

The maximum peak-to-trough drawdown was -44.4%, occurring from August 2011 to December 2015. This correction took approximately 52 months to unfold, underscoring the duration risk even in a secular bull market.

2. Volatility Analysis & Regime Detection

Volatility is measured as the annualized standard deviation of daily log returns, computed on rolling 21-day and 63-day windows. Regime classification uses the 63-day rolling volatility distribution: Low ≤ P25 (12.8%), Normal P25–P75, High P75–P90 (18.5%–24.3%), and Crisis > P90 (24.3%).

Key finding: Crisis-regime periods (>24% annualized vol) account for ~10% of trading days but exhibit meaningfully different return dynamics. High- and crisis-vol periods cluster around macro shocks (GFC 2008, COVID 2020, geopolitical escalations) and tend to persist — volatility is autocorrelated with a half-life of several weeks.

3. Seasonal & Calendar-Based Patterns

We test whether gold returns exhibit statistically meaningful seasonal patterns by month and day-of-week. A Kruskal-Wallis H-test across 12 monthly return groups yields H = 10.57, p = 0.4799 — insufficient evidence to reject the null of equal monthly distributions at the 5% level.

Jarque-Bera Normality (p=0.00e+00)

Gold's daily return distribution exhibits excess kurtosis of 7.02 (vs. 0 for a normal distribution), confirming significant fat tails. The Q-Q plot shows clear deviation from normality in both tails — extreme moves occur more frequently than Gaussian models predict. Skewness of -0.466 indicates a slight left skew. The Jarque-Bera test decisively rejects normality (p ≈ 0.0e+00).

Tail risk implication: At the 5% VaR level, an investor should expect a daily loss exceeding 1.76% roughly once per month. The CVaR (expected shortfall) of -2.64% indicates that when losses exceed the VaR threshold, they average 2.64% — about 1.5× the VaR level. Normal-distribution-based risk models will systematically understate gold's tail risk.

5. Momentum Dynamics & Liquidity Behavior

The 50/200-day moving average crossover system identifies 16 golden crosses and 16 death crosses over the full period. Golden crosses have historically preceded sustained rallies during the 2002–2011 and 2019–2026 bull phases, though whipsaws occurred in range-bound markets (2013–2018). The 20-day rate of change (ROC) provides a higher-frequency momentum lens; extreme ROC readings (> ±10%) tend to cluster during regime transitions.

Volume Analysis (post-2004)

Volume data is reliable from 2004 onward (earlier periods show systematic zeros). Trading volume has trended upward structurally, reflecting gold's growing role in institutional portfolios and ETF flows. Volume spikes typically coincide with price dislocations and volatility regime transitions — high volume confirms trend conviction, while declining volume during rallies can signal exhaustion.

6. Key Takeaways & Forward-Looking Considerations

1. Secular trend intact but extended. Gold's 12.4% CAGR over 25+ years masks significant drawdowns (-44% peak-to-trough). The post-2020 acceleration from ~$1,500 to ~$5,400 is the steepest sustained move in the dataset. Mean-reversion risk is elevated at current levels.
2. Volatility regimes are persistent and tradeable. The 63-day rolling vol cleanly separates four regimes. Regime transitions (particularly from Normal → High/Crisis) tend to coincide with macro shocks and offer risk management signals. Monitor the 63-day vol relative to the 19% threshold for early warning.
3. Fat tails demand non-Gaussian risk models. Excess kurtosis of 7.0 and a CVaR/VaR ratio of 1.5× mean that normal-distribution VaR underestimates tail risk by 30–50%. Use historical simulation or EVT-based approaches for gold allocation sizing.
4. Seasonal edges are statistically weak. The Kruskal-Wallis test fails to reject equal monthly distributions, suggesting that calendar-based timing strategies for gold lack robust statistical support.
5. Momentum signals are regime-dependent. MA crossover systems perform well in trending environments but generate false signals in range-bound markets. Combining momentum with volatility regime context improves signal quality. The current environment shows bullish MA alignment.
